## Epidemiology Begins With Occurrence and Distribution {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 3 -->

> “The study of the occurrence and distribution of health-related states or events in specified populations, including the study of the determinants influencing such states, and the application of this knowledge to control the health problems.”

<p class="source-line">Source: [@porta2008]</p>

## Measurement Makes Characteristics Observable {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 4 -->

::: {.grid-2 .align-center}
::: {.panel}
**MEASUREMENT**

- Observe and assign values to relevant characteristics.
- Look for patterns among those values.
:::

::: {.definition-copy}
> “The study of the occurrence and distribution of health-related states or events in specified populations, including the study of the determinants influencing such states, and the application of this knowledge to control the health problems.”
:::
:::

<p class="source-line">Source: [@porta2008]</p>

## Description Does Not Necessarily Seek Associations {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 8 -->

- Description examines distributions of single variables: middle, spread, shape, count, and proportion.
- It supports resource management and planning.
- Examples:
  - How many ventilators are available in Texas?
  - What is the average age of people living in Florida?
  - How much time elapses, on average, between exposure to a pathogen and the occurrence of disease symptoms?

## Description Can Also Compare Distributions {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 9 -->

- Sometimes description does look for associations.
- It may compare distributions of single variables within levels of another variable.
- Examples:
  - Are more ventilators available in Texas or New York?
  - Are people older, on average, in Florida or Pennsylvania?
  - Is symptom onset quicker, on average, for cholera or *E. coli*?

## Measures of Occurrence Support Description

<!-- Source PDF page 10 -->

- Counts
- Incidence
- Prevalence
- Odds

These measures can be useful on their own and for hypothesis generation.

## Occurrence Is Defined Within Populations {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 14 -->

> “The study of the occurrence and distribution of health-related states or events in specified **populations**, including the study of the determinants influencing such states, and the application of this knowledge to control the health problems.”

<p class="source-line">Source: [@porta2008]</p>

## Population

<!-- Source PDF page 15 -->

::: {.definition-copy}
> “The simplest definition of a **population** is a group of people who share characteristics or meet criteria that define membership in the population.”
:::

<p class="source-line">Source: [@lash2021]</p>

## A Population Also Has a Time Period

<!-- Source PDF page 16 -->

::: {.definition-copy}
> “The simplest definition of a **population** is a group of people **during a defined time period** who share characteristics or meet criteria that define membership in the population.”
:::

<p class="source-line">Source: [@lash2021]</p>

## Closed and Open Populations {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 17 -->

::: {.grid-2}
::: {.panel}
**CLOSED POPULATION**

- After the population is defined, it does not add new members over time.
- It loses members only to death.
:::

::: {.panel}
**OPEN POPULATION**

- It may gain members through birth or as people meet the membership definition.
- It loses members as people stop meeting the criteria or die.
:::
:::

<p class="source-line">Source: [@lash2021]</p>

## Examples of Closed and Open Populations {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 21 -->

- Currently enrolled in Epidemiology III: **open population**
- Ever enrolled in Epidemiology III as of today: **closed population**
- Resident of Texas: **open population**
- People aged 65 or older as of today: **closed population**
- People aged 20 to 30 as of today: **open population**

## Source and Target Populations {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 22 -->

**Source population:** The population from which persons will be sampled and included in a measurement of disease frequency.

- The source population of the original Framingham Heart Study included men and women aged 30 to 62 who were residents of Framingham, Massachusetts, in 1948.

**Target population:** The group of people about which the scientific or public-health question asks and for whom the disease-frequency information will be relevant, we hope.

- Information about cardiac-disease risk factors from the Framingham Heart Study contributed to a nearly 75% decline in cardiovascular-disease mortality in most industrialized societies.

<p class="source-line">Sources: [@lash2021; @westreich2019]</p>

## Study Population and Sample {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 23 -->

**Study population:** The subset, up to a complete census, of the source population whose experience is included in a measurement of disease frequency.

- In the Framingham Heart Study, not everyone eligible was invited and not everyone invited agreed. Those who were invited, agreed, and were free of prevalent cardiovascular disease constituted the study population.

**Sample:** A selected subset of a population. A sample may be random or nonrandom and representative or nonrepresentative.

<p class="source-line">Sources: [@lash2021; @porta2008]</p>

## Cohorts {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 24 -->

- A **cohort** is a group of persons whose membership is defined permanently, or a population in which satisfying a set of defining events makes membership permanent.
- The term is often used as a synonym for “sample” in a cohort study.
- Every cohort member is enumerated: known or listed. This is not necessarily true of a closed population.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@lash2021]</p>

## Measures Arise From Observations and Experiments {.study-design .compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 25 -->

| Measures | Design types | Typical evidential position |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Observations** | Case descriptions; ecological; cross-sectional; case-control; cohort | Typically less convincing |
| **Experiments** | Non-randomized; randomized | Typically more convincing |

## Terminology Recap: Population Types {.recap-table}

<!-- Source PDF page 26 -->

| Term | Definition | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Population | A group of people during a defined time period who share characteristics or meet membership criteria. | The population of the United States. |
| Closed population | After the population is defined, it adds no new members and loses members only to death. | People who had a flu vaccine in 2022. |
| Open population | During a defined time frame, it gains members through birth or newly met criteria and/or loses members when criteria are no longer met or through loss to follow-up. | People who have the flu. |

## Terminology Recap: Source and Target Populations {.recap-table}

<!-- Source PDF page 27 -->

| Term | Definition | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Source population | The population from which persons will be sampled and included in a measurement of disease frequency. | Men and women aged 30 to 62 who lived in Framingham, Massachusetts, in 1948. |
| Target population | The group addressed by the scientific or public-health question and for whom the disease-frequency information will be relevant, we hope. | Industrialized societies to which Framingham findings about cardiac-disease risk factors were applied. |

## Terminology Recap: Study Population and Sample {.recap-table}

<!-- Source PDF page 28 -->

| Term | Definition | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Study population | The subset, up to a census, of the source population whose experience is included in the measurement. | Framingham invitees who agreed to participate and were free of prevalent cardiovascular disease. |
| Sample | A selected subset of a population; it may be random or nonrandom and representative or nonrepresentative. | Another, probably more common, term for study population. |

## Terminology Recap: Cohort {.recap-table}

<!-- Source PDF page 29 -->

| Term | Definition | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Cohort | A group whose membership is permanent once a defining set of events is satisfied. A cohort may be open or closed and is often used as a synonym for “sample” in a cohort study. | Similar to a population, except every cohort member is enumerated: known or listed. |

## Prevalence Describes Existing Conditions {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 33 -->

- Prevalence provides information about the presence or absence of a condition of interest, such as a disease, exposure, or characteristic, in a population.
- It describes the extent to which the condition is present in a population during a given time frame.
- Asking about the prevalence of diabetes means asking how many, or more likely what proportion, of people currently living in the population have diabetes.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Prevalence Count {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 34 -->

- A count of people in a population with the condition of interest during a given time frame.
- As few as 0 people and as many as all people can be living with the condition.
- Range: 0 to infinity.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Prevalence Proportion {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 35 -->

- The proportion or percentage of the population that presently has the condition of interest or presently has a history of the condition during a specified period, such as a history of cancer in the past 10 years.
- Since none, some, or all population members can have the condition or a history of it, prevalence proportion ranges from 0 to 1, much like a probability.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Prevalence Proportion: Formula {.big-formula}

<!-- Source PDF page 36 -->

$$
\text{Prevalence proportion} = \frac{\text{Count with the condition}}{\text{Living members of the population}}
$$

## R {.r-divider}

<!-- Source PDF page 40 -->
<!-- REVIEW: The source PDF page contains only the R logo and its source URL; the intended exercise or demonstration content is not specified. -->

[**R**](https://www.r-project.org/)

## Point Prevalence and Period Prevalence {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 41 -->

- **Point prevalence:** prevalence of a condition of interest at a single point in time.
- **Period prevalence:** prevalence of a condition of interest over a period of time.
- As the duration of the period shrinks, period prevalence converges to point prevalence.
- There is no hard-and-fast rule for what window is sufficiently short to count as point prevalence.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Prevalence Odds {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 42 -->

- Prevalence odds is a simple function of prevalence proportion, just as odds in general is a simple function of probability.
- It is typically reported for convenience or desirable statistical properties.
- Prevalence odds is prevalence proportion divided by 1 minus prevalence proportion.
- Range: 0 to infinity.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Prevalence Odds: Formula {.big-formula}

<!-- Source PDF page 43 -->

$$
\text{Prevalence odds} = \frac{\text{Prevalence proportion}}{1 - \text{Prevalence proportion}}
$$

## Prevalence Odds at Month 2 {.big-formula}

<!-- Source PDF page 44 -->

$$
\text{Prevalence odds} = \frac{0.20}{1 - 0.20} = 0.25
$$

## Interpreting Prevalence Odds

<!-- Source PDF page 45 -->

Among the members of the population, the odds of disease in month 2 were **0.25**.

For every person who had disease at month 2, there were four people who did not.

## Incidence Describes New Occurrences {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 47 -->

- Prevalence measures how many cases are present at a moment or over a period; incidence measures how many **new cases** arise over a specified period.
- Unlike prevalence, incidence measures occurrences or events: transitions from a condition being absent in an individual to the condition being present over a specified period.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Incidence Proportion and Risk

<!-- Source PDF page 48 -->

- Incidence proportion and “risk” are sometimes used interchangeably in epidemiology.
- Risk can be ambiguous. Incidence proportion is less so.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Incidence Count {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 49 -->

- A count of new occurrences of a condition in a population at risk for the occurrence during a given time frame.
- Range: 0 to infinity.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Incidence Proportion {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 50 -->

- The proportion of the population that experiences a new occurrence of the condition among those at risk of experiencing a new occurrence during a given time frame.
- Like all proportions, it falls between 0 and 1.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Incidence Proportion: Formula {.big-formula}

<!-- Source PDF page 51 -->

$$
\text{Incidence proportion} = \frac{\text{Count of new occurrences}}{\text{Population at risk}}
$$

| Person | At risk | New disease | Deceased |
|---:|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | 0 months | Prevalent before follow-up | — |
| 2 | 0–2 | Month 2 | 5–12 |
| 3 | 0–4 | Month 4 | — |
| 4 | 0–5 | Month 5 | — |
| 5 | 0–7 | Month 7 | — |
| 6 | 0–8 | Month 8 | 11–12 |
| 7 | 0–9 | — | 9–12 |
| 8 | 0–5 | — | 5–12 |

## Incidence Proportion Over 12 Months {.metric-grid}

<!-- Source PDF page 53 -->

::: {.grid-2 .align-center}
::: {.status-summary}
- 5 people developed disease.
- 9 people were at risk at baseline.
- Person 1 was already diseased and therefore not at risk for a new occurrence.
:::

::: {.big-formula}
$$
\frac{5}{9} = 0.56 = 56\%
$$
:::
:::

## Interpreting Incidence Proportion

<!-- Source PDF page 54 -->

Among the members of the population, the incidence of disease over 12 months of follow-up was **0.56**.

Fifty-six percent of the population developed disease over 12 months of follow-up.

## Incidence Odds: Formula {.big-formula}

<!-- Source PDF page 55 -->

$$
\text{Incidence odds} = \frac{\text{Incidence proportion}}{1 - \text{Incidence proportion}}
$$

## Incidence Odds Over 12 Months {.big-formula}

<!-- Source PDF page 56 -->

$$
\text{Incidence odds} = \frac{0.56}{1 - 0.56} = 1.27
$$

## Interpreting Incidence Odds {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 57 -->

Among the members of the population, the odds of incident disease over 12 months of follow-up were **1.27**.

For every 127 people who developed incident disease over 12 months of follow-up, 100 people did not.

## Incidence Rate {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 58 -->

- A measure of the average intensity at which an event occurs in people's experience over time.
- For a population followed from baseline, it is the number of cases divided by the person-time at risk accumulated by the population.
- Range: 0 to infinity.
- **Not a proportion.**
- The denominator is reciprocal time, usually person-time.
- The numeric value depends on the selected time unit and therefore has no interpretation by itself.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Person-Time

<!-- Source PDF page 59 -->

**Person-time** is the amount of time observed for all people under study while they are at risk of experiencing an incident outcome.

<p class="source-line">Source: [@westreich2019]</p>

## Follow-Up Experience and Time at Risk {.status-table}

<!-- Source PDF page 60 -->

| Person | Time at risk | Outcome after risk time |
|---:|---:|:---|
| 1 | 0 months | Prevalent disease |
| 2 | 2 months | Disease, then death |
| 3 | 4 months | Disease |
| 4 | 5 months | Disease |
| 5 | 7 months | Disease |
| 6 | 8 months | Disease, then death |
| 7 | 9 months | Death |
| 8 | 5 months | Death |
| 9 | 12 months | None observed |
| 10 | 12 months | None observed |

<p class="source-line">Source: [@lash2021]</p>

## Calculating Person-Time {.metric-grid}

<!-- Source PDF page 61 -->

$$
\sum_{\text{people}} \text{Time at risk}
$$

$$
0 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 5 + 12 + 12 = 64\text{ person-months}
$$

## Interpreting Person-Time

<!-- Source PDF page 62 -->

The population accumulated **64 person-months at risk** during 12 months of follow-up.

The same amount is **5.33 person-years at risk** during 12 months of follow-up.

## Follow-Up Experience for the Incidence Rate {.status-table}

<!-- Source PDF page 63 -->

| Person | Time at risk | New occurrence? |
|---:|---:|:---:|
| 1 | 0 months | No; prevalent |
| 2 | 2 months | Yes |
| 3 | 4 months | Yes |
| 4 | 5 months | Yes |
| 5 | 7 months | Yes |
| 6 | 8 months | Yes |
| 7 | 9 months | No |
| 8 | 5 months | No |
| 9 | 12 months | No |
| 10 | 12 months | No |

<p class="source-line">Source: [@lash2021]</p>

## Incidence Rate: Calculation {.big-formula}

<!-- Source PDF page 64 -->

$$
\text{Incidence rate} = \frac{\text{Count of new occurrences}}{\text{Person-time at risk}}
$$

$$
= \frac{5}{64\text{ person-months}} \approx 7.8\text{ per 100 person-months}
$$

## Interpreting the Incidence Rate {.compact}

<!-- Source PDF page 65 -->

The incidence rate of disease among the members of the population was **5 cases per 64 person-months** during 12 months of follow-up.

Equivalently, the incidence rate was **7.8 cases per 100 person-months** during 12 months of follow-up.

## Odds and Proportions {.odds-table}

<!-- Source PDF page 66 -->

$$
\text{Odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}
$$

| $p$ | Odds |
|---:|---:|
| 0.01 | 0.010 |
